messages.subject: Re: Detections in infrared
messages.body_plain:
Hi Murray,

Yes, you are correct about the secr.fit call. More specifically we have secr.fit(CH, model = list(D = ~1, g0 = ~1, sigma = ~1, pID = ~daynight), mask = mask, trace = FALSE, details = list(knownmarks = FALSE, nsim = 10000)). Our daynight covariate consists of character values of N/Y for day/night. In the secr-multisession vignette, it says that if sessions are not independent, then CIs will likely be narrow. This is why we decided to bootstrap. However, all of that being said, I think formatting our data as a single session and including the "timecov" argument in secr.fit or creating a trap covariate would be more straightforward. Thank you for the ideas.

messages.subject: Understanding sigma
messages.body_plain:
Hi Murray,

I'm hoping to clarify exactly what a Sigma value means. As far as I know, Sigma is defined as the spatial scale of detection function (in meters) that determines the rate at which the probability of detection decreases with distance and is related to the home-range area of individuals. Does a Sigma value of 80m mean that on average the detection probability of individuals is halved (50%) when they are 80m away from their home-range centre? I'm studying short-eared possums (Trichosurus caninus) btw.

Cheers,
Lachlan

messages.subject: Citations compare secr.fit and openCR.fit
messages.body_plain:
Hi Murray,

I prefer to use openCR.fit over secr.fit for a lot of my abundance estimates. I have relatively long lived species (13+ years for boodies) that are really trap happy, monitored twice a year, and contained within a fenced enclosure. Despite the lack of GOF testing in openCR I’m convinced it does a better job of estimating abundance because it acknowledges that my populations are open temporally.

That said, journal reviewers with experience in Program MARK are being a real pain in the butt asking for AIC tables to prove that individual covariates should be included (or not). I haven’t used trap covariates (yet) because I work in a fenced enclosure and we know that boodies in particular will travel well outside their normal range for peanut butter.

Can you please suggest some citations for responding to these sorts of comments from reviewers? If I recall correctly, there is a PhD thesis produced during the development of openCR?

Thanks,

Cheryl

messages.subject: Re: Understanding sigma
messages.body_plain:
I'd hesitate to interpret sigma in such concrete terms. It is the spatial scale parameter of a particular detection model. I imagine you are using a halfnormal model. The probability is for capture in a particular trap in the absence of any competing traps. Then I get

r <- 80                               # distance from activity centre
sigma <- 80
p <- exp(-r^2/(2*sigma^2))   # half normal, ignoring g0 for probability relative to centre
p
[1] 0.6065307

Which is not 0.5. Use a different detection function and you'll get a different p result for given r, even when both give similar density estimates.

messages.body_plain:
Cheryl
There's no thesis relating to openCR, just the Efford & Schofield Biometrics paper.
I don't quite understand your problem. You can do AIC with openCR, can't you? I tend to think openCR is better kept for questions on survival, recruitment and movement. Sorry to complicate things by questioning your chosen path. Either way I have a fairly aggressive view towards model selection pedants: at some point you make a biologically informed judgement on what matters and go with that.
Murray

messages.subject: Multisession maks in multisession OpenCR
messages.body_plain:
Hello everyone,

I have a dataset that I'm analysing on spatial and non spatial OpenCr. The data consists of inter-annual data between 2015 and 2020, hence i've created a multisession object were each year is a primary session. The main parameter I want to calculate is time specific density. Since distance between movements and detections vary within years, the mask is different for each year.

When i run the multisession object the program realises that there are different masks and just defaults to the first one, instead of using the yearly specific mask for each of the yearly calculations. I'm unsure of how to get around this, do i just need to separate the object into single sessions per year? although this would provide estimates between months instead a whole value for the year itself.

Any insights on the above would greatly appreciated.

Cheers,

Diana

messages.subject: Re: Multisession maks in multisession OpenCR
messages.body_plain:
Diana
" Since distance between movements and detections vary within years, the mask is different for each year." ? I don't think you make a case, and this cannot be done in 'openCR'. The primary sessions are merged ('joined') into a single-session object for analysis, and the code does not allow a time-varying mask extent. Just go with a mask that is generous enough for the primary session with the largest movement, with a larger buffer if you think there is between-session movement of centres. Of course the mask is not relevant for nonspatial models.
Murray

messages.subject: Re: Spatially explicit mark resight models
messages.body_plain:
Andreu
The case of 'sightings only when the number marked is unknown' (Section 4.2 in Efford & Hunter 2017) can be problematic. Warnings 1-7 arise because the number of individuals observed (n) is more than actually present in the model for the parameter values at that step in the likelihood maximisation. It can probably be ignored if the algorithm goes on to produce estimates. The last warning (8) often reflects trouble in estimating the variances, so to be safe I would recalculate those with
fit.HN2 <- secr.fit (CH, mask = Pianosamask, detectfn = 'HN',  start = fit.HN, method = 'none',

                     trace = FALSE,fixed = list(pID = 1.0),details = list(knownmarks = TRUE))

This applies a better algorithm.
Murray
